noteRef.topicTitle: 1. Structure, Bonding & Introduction to Organic Chemistry

specPoints.text: understand the effects of ionic radius and ionic charge on the strength of ionic bonding
understand reasons for the trends in ionic radii down a group in the Periodic Table, and for a set of isoelectronic ions, including N 3− to Al 3+

primer.text: Radii set the grip. Across period 3 atoms contract as nuclear charge climbs against constant shielding; ions shrink or swell with charge sign; and isoelectronic ions - one shared electron cloud - tighten as protons accumulate. Bond strength follows charge density, so higher charges on smaller ions bind hardest. This note runs all three radius rules and their strength consequences.

lessons.title: Measuring and shrinking the atom
lessons.opening: Atomic radius means the span from the nucleus to the outermost electron, measured by halving the nucleus-to-nucleus distance between two bonded atoms of the same element. Across period 3 the radius steadily contracts: every extra proton pulls the same shell inward while shielding stays level, so the atoms shrink from sodium to argon.
keyPoints: Atomic radius is the nucleus-to-outermost-electron distance, found by halving the internuclear distance of two like atoms.
In metals the measure is the metallic radius; in non-metals it is the covalent radius.
Nuclear charge and electron count each rise by one per step, with the same number of shells throughout.
The stronger pull draws the unchanged shell closer, contracting the atom step by step.

low.restatement: Take half the gap between two identical bonded atoms and you have the radius; across a period that half-gap keeps shrinking as the nucleus gains protons.
low.analogy: Two tennis balls pressed together: half their centre-to-centre spacing is each ball's radius - and across a period the balls keep shrinking while staying in the same row.
low.examPointer: Quote the trio - charge up, shielding constant, pull stronger - when asked why radii fall across a period.

medium.restatement: Across period 3 each element adds one proton and one electron to the same principal shell; screening is therefore unchanged and the growing nuclear charge draws the shell inward, so radii contract monotonically.
medium.analogy: Twelve spotlights (protons) illuminating the same stage (shell): each new spotlight tightens the ensemble without adding a row to the theatre.
medium.examPointer: Distinguish metallic radius from covalent radius by element type - the terms ride on whether the bonded element is a metal.

check.stem: How is the atomic radius of an element obtained?

options.text: Halving the measured distance between the nuclei of two bonded atoms of the element
options.explanation: Half the internuclear spacing is each atom's share.

options.text: Measuring from nucleus to the nearest inner shell
options.explanation: The definition uses the outermost electron, not an inner shell.

options.text: Weighing one mole of the atoms
options.explanation: Molar mass carries no spatial information.

options.text: Reading it directly off the periodic table
options.explanation: The table arranges elements; radii come from measurement.

check.stem: What happens to atomic radii across period 3?

options.text: They decrease steadily from sodium to argon
options.explanation: Rising nuclear charge with constant shielding contracts each atom.

options.text: They increase steadily
options.explanation: The increase belongs to the down-group direction.

options.text: They stay the same because shells are constant
options.explanation: Constant shells fix shielding but not the radius.

options.text: They jump up at every group boundary
options.explanation: No jumps appear across a period.

check.stem: Why does shielding stay effectively constant across a period?

options.text: Electrons are added to the same principal shell
options.explanation: No new inner shell appears, so screening by inner electrons is unchanged.

options.text: Electrons are removed one at a time
options.explanation: Electron count rises across a period.

options.text: Protons and neutrons cancel each other
options.explanation: Neutrons play no screening role here.

options.text: The nucleus shrinks as charge grows
options.explanation: The nucleus does not shrink; it attracts harder.

check.stem: Which pair of quantities rises together across period 3?

options.text: Nuclear charge and electron count
options.explanation: Each step adds one proton and one electron.

options.text: Atomic radius and shielding
options.explanation: Radius falls while shielding stays level.

options.text: Shell count and radius
options.explanation: Shell count is fixed within the period.

options.text: Metallic radius and covalent radius
options.explanation: These are alternative measures for different element types, not co-rising quantities.

check.stem: What name does the atomic radius take when the bonded element is a non-metal?

options.text: The covalent radius
options.explanation: Non-metals bond covalently, so their radius measure takes that name.

options.text: The metallic radius
options.explanation: That name belongs to metals.

options.text: The ionic radius
options.explanation: Ionic radius measures ions, not neutral atoms.

options.text: The van der Waals radius
options.explanation: That is a different contact-based measure.

check.stem: Define the atomic radius in terms of a measurement between two atoms.
check.modelAnswer: To get the atomic radius, measure the internuclear gap between two atoms of the same element and halve it - half that gap is the nucleus-to-outermost-electron span.

check.stem: State the trend in atomic radius across period 3 and the two constant factors behind it.
check.modelAnswer: Atomic radii decrease across period 3 because proton and electron counts rise one per step while the shell count - and therefore shielding - stays constant.

check.stem: Explain why adding electrons across a period does not enlarge the atom.
check.modelAnswer: Each added electron joins the existing outer shell rather than a new one, so screening does not relax; meanwhile the extra nuclear charge pulls harder on the same shell, drawing it inward and shrinking the atom.

check.stem: Predict, with your reasoning, which period-3 element holds the smallest atomic radius and where the largest sits.
check.modelAnswer: Argon is smallest - by period's end the nuclear charge is largest against the same shell - and sodium is largest, holding the weakest pull at the period's start.

lessons.title: Ionic radius obeys the charge
lessons.opening: Ion formation resizes the atom in a direction set by the charge. Gaining electrons swells the radius - the extra electrons sit further out and are held weakly - while losing electrons shrinks it, because the untouched nucleus now pulls fewer electrons harder. Ionic bond strength then follows charge density: higher charges and smaller radii forge stronger bonds.
keyPoints: Ionic radius measures the size of an ion.
Radii increase with increasing negative charge and decrease with increasing positive charge.
Negative ions form by gaining electrons; the outermost electrons sit further out and are weakly held.
Positive ions form by losing electrons; the unchanged nucleus attracts the reduced electron set more strongly.
Stronger ionic bonds come from higher charges and smaller sizes, which raise the charge density.

low.restatement: Add electrons and the ion bulges; remove electrons and it tightens around the same nucleus. Bigger charges packed into smaller ions bind hardest.
low.analogy: Overstuffing a suitcase spreads it open (anion); emptying it lets the frame compress (cation).
low.examPointer: Direction questions hinge on sign: more negative means larger, more positive means smaller.

medium.restatement: Radius shifts follow the electrostatic ledger: gained electrons raise mutual repulsion and stretch the ion, while electron loss leaves the proton count unchanged over fewer electrons, deepening per-electron attraction; bond strength scales with charge density, charge over size.
medium.analogy: A landlord (nucleus) with fixed strength squeezing fewer tenants (electrons) presses each one closer; more tenants crowd outward.
medium.examPointer: Link the radius rules to bond strength through charge density - that chain is what the ionic-bond-strength question wants.

check.stem: What happens to ionic radius as negative charge increases?

options.text: It increases - more electrons push the outer shell outward
options.explanation: Gained electrons are held weakly further from the nucleus.

options.text: It decreases - extra charge pulls electrons in
options.explanation: Negative charge means gained electrons, which expand the ion.

options.text: It stays constant with charge
options.explanation: Radius tracks charge systematically.

options.text: It changes only for metals
options.explanation: The rule covers anions of non-metals generally.

check.stem: Why do positive ions have smaller radii than their parent atoms?

options.text: Electron loss leaves the same nucleus attracting fewer electrons more strongly
options.explanation: Per-electron attraction deepens after electrons are removed.

options.text: The nucleus loses protons during ionisation
options.explanation: Proton count is untouched by electron loss.

options.text: Gained electrons crowd the shell outward
options.explanation: Positive ions lose electrons; they gain none.

options.text: Neutrons escape to shrink the nucleus
options.explanation: Neutrons stay put and carry no charge.

check.stem: Which combination produces the strongest ionic bonding?

options.text: High ionic charges with small ionic radii
options.explanation: Charge density - charge over size - peaks with big charges on small ions.

options.text: Low charges with large radii
options.explanation: That combination minimises charge density.

options.text: Equal charges with equal radii
options.explanation: Matched mediocrity beats nothing special.

options.text: Large radii with high charges only on one ion
options.explanation: Bond strength reads the pair together; sizes and charges both matter.

check.stem: Charge density of a cation increases when

options.text: its charge rises or its radius falls
options.explanation: Both movements raise charge over surface area.

options.text: its charge falls or its radius grows
options.explanation: Both movements dilute the density.

options.text: its neutron count rises
options.explanation: Neutrons do not enter the charge density.

options.text: its mass number increases
options.explanation: Mass is not part of charge density.

check.stem: A lattice of 2+ and 2- ions melts far higher than a 1+/1- lattice of similar ion size because

options.text: the doubled charges raise the electrostatic attraction throughout the lattice
options.explanation: Each contact pulls harder, so much more energy is needed to flow.

options.text: doubly charged ions are always smaller
options.explanation: Size similarity was given; charge is the deciding difference.

options.text: extra electrons roam and add bonding
options.explanation: Ionic lattices have no delocalised electrons.

options.text: the higher charge weakens repulsion entirely
options.explanation: Repulsion still exists; net attraction is what strengthened.

check.stem: State the two radius rules for increasing negative and increasing positive charge.
check.modelAnswer: Ionic radii increase with increasing negative charge and decrease with increasing positive charge.

check.stem: State the two ion properties that raise the strength of an ionic bond.
check.modelAnswer: Higher ionic charges and smaller ionic sizes produce stronger ionic bonds by raising the charge density.

check.stem: Explain why the outermost electrons of an anion are held only weakly.
check.modelAnswer: Gained electrons occupy the outermost region, further from the positive nucleus and screened by all the inner electrons, so each one feels a reduced pull and the ion swells.

check.stem: Arrange O2-, F-, and Na+ - all with the same electron count - by ionic radius and give the rule at the turning point.
check.modelAnswer: O2- > F- > Na+: the same electron cloud tightens as proton count rises from 8 to 9 to 11; crossing from negative to positive charge flips the radius rule, shrinking the cation below both anions.

lessons.title: Isoelectronic ions: same cloud, different grip
lessons.opening: Isoelectronic ions share one electronic configuration - the series N3-, O2-, F-, Na+, Mg2+, Al3+ all carry 1s2 2s2 2p6 - yet their radii are not equal. More protons behind the identical cloud mean a tighter pull, so the radius falls step by step from the nitride ion's 0.171 nm to the aluminium ion's 0.054 nm.
keyPoints: Isoelectronic ions have the same electronic configuration.
N3-, O2-, F-, Na+, Mg2+ and Al3+ all share the 1s2 2s2 2p6 arrangement.
The ions differ in proton number: 7, 8, 9, 11, 12 and 13.
More protons pull the same electron cloud closer, so radii fall across the series.
The spread runs from N3- at 0.171 nm down to Al3+ at 0.054 nm.

low.restatement: Same electrons, different nuclei: the ion with the most protons squeezes the shared cloud tightest, so the sizes slide downhill as charge climbs.
low.analogy: The same blanket pulled by beds of increasing width - the widest bed (most protons) stretches the blanket flattest and smallest.
low.examPointer: List the series with proton counts when explaining - the counts are the whole argument.

medium.restatement: With the electron cloud fixed, radius becomes a pure function of nuclear charge: each added proton deepens the per-electron attraction, contracting the identical configuration from 0.171 nm at seven protons to 0.054 nm at thirteen.
medium.analogy: One fixed cast of actors on stages of increasing grip: the director's insistence (proton count) compresses the same play into ever-smaller stages.
medium.examPointer: The isoelectronic series is the examiner's favourite trap - compare radii by protons, never by ion sign alone.

check.stem: What defines a set of isoelectronic ions?

options.text: They share the same electronic configuration
options.explanation: Identical electron arrangements with different nuclei.

options.text: They carry the same ionic charge
options.explanation: The series spans 3- to 3+; charges differ.

options.text: They have the same number of protons
options.explanation: Proton counts run 7 to 13 across the series.

options.text: They have identical ionic radii
options.explanation: Radii fall systematically across the series.

check.stem: Which configuration do N3-, O2-, F-, Na+, Mg2+ and Al3+ all share?

options.explanation: Ten electrons in three subshells, the neon arrangement.
That is short two electrons of the shared set.
That adds a shell none of the ions carries.
Far too few electrons for the series.

check.stem: Why does ionic radius fall across the isoelectronic series?

options.text: Proton count rises while the electron cloud stays identical
options.explanation: More nuclear charge grips the same ten electrons more tightly.

options.text: Electrons are lost at each step
options.explanation: The configuration is constant; no electrons leave.

options.text: New shells open as charge grows
options.explanation: The shared configuration has no shell changes.

options.text: Neutrons accumulate and press inward
options.explanation: Neutrons carry no charge and take no part.

check.stem: Which member of the isoelectronic series has the largest ionic radius?

options.text: N3-, with only seven protons
options.explanation: The fewest protons grip the shared cloud loosest, at 0.171 nm.

options.text: Al3+, with thirteen protons
options.explanation: Aluminium grips hardest and is smallest at 0.054 nm.

options.text: Na+, the neutral midpoint
options.explanation: Eleven protons sit mid-series, mid-radius.

options.text: All six tie at the same radius
options.explanation: Radii differ despite identical configurations.

check.stem: The ionic radius of Al3+ is 0.054 nm against N3-'s 0.171 nm. Roughly how many times smaller is the aluminium ion?

options.text: About 3.2 times smaller
About 6 times smaller
options.explanation: That divides by the proton gap of 6, not the radii.

options.text: About 1.6 times smaller
options.explanation: That misreads the ratio as roughly half.

options.text: They are equal
options.explanation: The quoted values differ by a factor of three.

check.stem: Define isoelectronic ions.
check.modelAnswer: Isoelectronic ions are ions that share the same electronic configuration, such as N3-, O2-, F-, Na+, Mg2+ and Al3+.

check.stem: State the proton counts of N3- and Al3+ and their ionic radii in nm.
check.modelAnswer: N3- carries 7 protons with a radius of 0.171 nm; Al3+ carries 13 protons with a radius of 0.054 nm.

check.stem: Explain why identical electron configurations do not force identical ionic radii.
check.modelAnswer: Radius depends on the balance between nuclear pull and electron repulsion; with the electron cloud fixed, the nucleus with more protons attracts each electron harder, contracting its ion relative to its neighbours in the series.

check.stem: Place Mg2+ in order within the isoelectronic series by radius, with reasoning from proton counts.
check.modelAnswer: Mg2+ with 12 protons sits second smallest - above Al3+ (13 protons, smallest) and below Na+ (11 protons) - because every extra proton tightens the shared 1s2 2s2 2p6 cloud.

glossary.definition: The distance from the nucleus to the outermost electron, taken as half the internuclear distance between two like bonded atoms.
The measure of an ion's size, which grows with negative charge and shrinks with positive charge.
The ionic charge relative to the ion's surface area; higher density means stronger ionic bonding.
Sharing the same electronic configuration while differing in nuclear charge.
